reasons: Uses real saved match files, not only invented data.
Tests both valid data and specific kinds of broken data.
Checks rain and super-over handling as well as normal matches.

terms.meaning: A public source of ball-by-ball cricket match data.
A saved sample file used by tests so they run the same way every time.
A delivery that counts toward the six balls of an over. Wides and no-balls do not count.
A data problem the checks found, such as deliveries out of order.
A short decider played when a match is tied.

sections.name: File setup, load
sections.title: Loads saved match files
sections.what: Finds every match file in the fixtures folder and converts each one into the app's format, using the match number as its name.
sections.why: Likely reason: the other tests work on the same converted matches, so the loading is shared in one place.
sections.watch_out: If the fixtures folder is missing, the list is empty and loops pass silently, so only the first test would flag it.

sections.name: data contract on real Cricsheet fixtures
sections.title: Checks match data quality
sections.what: Checks there are at least five matches including a tie and a rain-affected match. Checks every match passes the data checks. Checks that rain-affected chases are excluded from analysis, tied matches decided by super over are valid, and broken copies are caught: out-of-order deliveries, too many legal balls, a wrong winner, negative runs, and a chase shortened to 10 overs without a recorded reason.
sections.why: Likely reason: the analysis depends on clean match records, so bad data must be caught before it reaches the app.
sections.watch_out: The broken-copy tests use the first match that has a winner and no method, so changes to the fixtures can silently change which match is tested.

summary: Tests that the saved Cricsheet match files pass data checks, and that broken data is caught.
purpose: Makes sure only trustworthy match data reaches the app, and that matches with rain interruptions are not used for chase analysis.
why: Likely reason: bad data would produce wrong chase numbers, so the checks run on real saved match files before the app relies on them.
how: Finds all match files in data/fixtures/cricsheet. Parses each one into the app's format. Runs the data checks and expects no violations. Checks that a tie and a rain-affected match are present and handled. Then builds deliberately broken copies of one match and confirms each break is reported.
inputs: Saved Cricsheet match files in data/fixtures/cricsheet, one per match, named by match number.
outputs: Pass or fail results. The data checks return a list of violations and whether the match can be used for chase analysis, with reasons.
risks: If the fixtures folder is missing, the file list is empty and per-file loops pass without checking anything. The first test catches this. Broken-copy tests pick a match by rule, so changing the fixtures can change which match they use.
debug: If a test fails, read the violation text it prints for that match file. Check the Cricsheet parser and the contract checks. Confirm the fixtures folder has files.
